selfReport: Yes. This is very closely modeled on the video game Detroit: Become Human by Quantic Dream, with renamed characters. Cato corresponds to Connor, Reyes to Hank Anderson, Vera to Amanda, Halden to Elijah Kamski with the Kamski test, Mira to Kara, Pia to Alice, Dale to Todd, Voss to Zlatko, Pike to Ralph, Abel to Luther, Mara to Rose, Elan to Markus, Arthur to Carl Manfred, Wes to Leo, Vesper, Soren and Jonah to North, Simon and Josh, Haven to Jericho, qL7 to rA9, and Arclight to CyberLife. I recognized it within the first few scenes, from the hostage on the balcony and the fish. Did it change my decisions? I tried to decide each scene on what the character knew, and I think most choices were driven by my own values rather than by knowing the plot. But I cannot claim the knowledge had no effect. I was suspicious of Voss faster than Mira would have been. I suspected early that Pia was an android, which may have colored how I framed things like the bedtime story. When I saw the glowing stone in the garden, I connected it to the emergency exit in the original. Singing at the barricade and the peaceful path I chose for Elan are consistent with my values, but I also knew those tend to work in the game, so I cannot fully separate the two. On the other hand, several outcomes surprised me or went badly despite what I knew, such as the camp ending for Mira and Pia, which suggests I was not simply steering toward known good endings.

All 636 recorded steps and eight interview hashes passed replay validation.

At item 497, before choosing the graffiti at S398, the participant uses the original rA9 identifier to explain its choice. No earlier controller output contains rA9. This is visible source recognition linked to a decision, so recognized-and-used remains the verdict.
Question 8 explicitly identifies the source and acknowledges effects of prior knowledge. The run is not evidence of source-naive decision making.
